newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Communist foes take on Yeltsin over health.
newsitem.headline: Communist foes take on Yeltsin over health.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's communist rivals have seized upon a controversy surrounding his planned heart surgery, urging the Russian leader to quit if he proves too ill to rule.
The communist speaker of the State Duma lower house of parliament said Yeltsin, 65, should resign if the surgeons refused to operate and told him to take life easy.
"The situation in Russia is such that (the president) cannot have an easy work schedule," Gennady Seleznyov told reporters.
Yeltsin disappeared from public in June, right in the middle of a fierce re-election campaign which brought him a victory over the Communist contender, Gennady Zyuganov.
Earlier this month Yeltsin, whose aides had said was simply overtired by campaigning, suddenly announced that he had agreed to bypass surgery to improve the blood supply to his heart.
He said in a televised interview the operation was likely to take place in late September.

Yeltsin's announcement has sparked speculations about the actual state of his health -- further fuelled this weekend when a top doctor, Renat Akchurin, who is expected to to lead the operation, suggested that surgery might be delayed for six to eight weeks, or even cancelled altogether.
Zyuganov said the doctor's remark that Yeltsin probably had a heart attack during the campaign showed that the Kremlin had deceived voters.
"(Concealing the heart attack) amounts to falsification. The elections were not fair," he told Reuters at the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly in Strasbourg.
Russian share prices fell over three percent on news of the likely delay.
Russian debt took a nosedive on international markets on Monday. Russian shares and bonds also fell.

Yeltsin's press secretary put the blame on an article published in the Financial Times newspaper on Monday which alleged that the Kremlin leader had a 50:50 chance of surviving the surgery and could work only 15 minutes a day.

"The London Financial Times today published an article about the state of health of the Russian president which... contains a completely false assertion that 'Yeltsin can work only 15 minutes a day'," Sergei Yastrzhembsky said in a statement.
"The article also contains other assertions which have nothing to do with reality."
He said the report had apparently caused a considerable fall in Russia's foreign debt prices on the London securities market.
Denying the newspaper report, the Kremlin had little to say about the actual state of Yeltsin's health.
A Kremlin spokesman said there may be no comment until a council of doctors, including foreign experts, meets on Wednesday to decide when or whether to operate.
Russians, and governments abroad, are left guessing about who is running the nuclear superpower, which still has a fragile grip on democracy five years after the Soviet Union fell apart.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who would take over to organise new elections if Yeltsin were to step down, has been given some extra duties and will take over full presidential powers for the few hours Yeltsin is on the operating table.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted Chernomyrdin's press office as saying that he and Yeltsin would hold a routine working meeting on Tuesday. It gave no details about the agenda of the meeting.
